title: How could a programme be hidden from Congress?

lead.text: What the board documents is the lawful machinery, not a programme using it: for the Department of Defense, 10 U.S.C. 119 lets the Secretary send a waived programme's details only to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of six defense committees, and a carve-out, approved only by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary, removes outside industrial security inspection of a programme held at a contractor.

answer.text: Subsection (e) of section 119 has been in force unamended since 1987. It lets the Secretary personally waive, case by case, any requirement that information be included in a report, with no time limit, no periodic re-justification and no congressional ability to disapprove; the withheld information goes jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each defense committee.

Nothing in section 119 requires that waived information be delivered in writing, recorded, retained or shared with other members, and the Moynihan Commission recorded in 1997 that for waived programmes the chair, ranking member and occasionally others were notified only orally.

The covert action rule has safeguards the waived-SAP rule lacks: within 180 days of a limited notification the President must widen access or re-justify it, and all members of the intelligence committee must be told that a limited notification occurred. Section 119 has neither, so defense committee members outside the group are not told a waiver has been used.

House Oversight, which held the UAP hearings of July 2023, November 2024 and September 2025, is not a defense committee and receives nothing under section 119. Its chairwoman said on the record in September 2025 that the Department had told committee staff only members of House Armed Services and the House Appropriations defense subcommittee could be read in on such programmes.
Whether any UAP programme sits behind this machinery the board cannot show. What it can show is where the seams are; that a programme uses them is testimony and inference.

for.text: A carve-out removes three things at once: DCSA's security inspections at the contractor's site, its authorisation of the programme's computer systems, and its counterintelligence cross-sharing. On the board's reading this is the smallest documented arrangement in which a private company can hold classified material with no inspection by anyone outside the programme.

The one open audit of a special access contract found the controls weak: GAO testified in 1986 that Lockheed reported 1,460 discrepancies in an inventory of about 40,000 secret and top-secret items, told the Secretary the failure might not have occurred had the Defense Investigative Service been allowed to inspect, and called it inconsistent to protect a special access programme less well than a normal one.

GAO's 2004 audit of industrial security found DoD could not provide adequate assurance that its oversight of more than 11,000 contractor facilities protected classified information, and by agreement with committee staff it did not examine special access programmes at contractor facilities at all.

The paper for a waived programme stays inside the Department: justification materials go only to committee staff directors, waived SAP material submitted to Congress stays in DoD custody, and DoD SAPCO must approve any contractor's disclosure to Congress and keeps the record of what Congress was given.

David Grusch testified that he had been tasked to identify the special and controlled access programmes the UAP Task Force needed and was denied the read-ons he asked for; this is his sworn account, and the programmes he sought have not been named on the record.

Members of Congress describe the access problem in their own words: Burlison said the Department was not transparent to members even in a SCIF and that if you want to hide something from Congress you hand it to a private contractor, and Luna said programme budgets and oversight reporting are classified and go only to the authorising and appropriations committees.

On the board's reading the four reporting regimes leave seams with no annual census running to a full committee: a DoD programme under a waiver, and anything protected by Alternative Compensatory Control Measures rather than SAP controls. That is an inference from the statutes, not a record of any programme using them.

against.text: A waiver redirects reporting rather than ending it: the withheld information goes to the twelve seat holders together with the justification, and DoD's instruction states that waived programmes remain subject to congressional oversight. On the board's own reading of the statute, a programme never notified to the committees at all would not be a lawful waived programme but an unreported one.

A carve-out does not end all oversight: substitute procedures must meet the industrial security manual's standards and frequency, the facility still holds a DCSA-issued clearance and so still exists in DCSA's records, and waived programmes are reviewed each year.

A carve-out is not invisible inside the Department: only the Secretary or Deputy Secretary can approve one, each SAP record file must hold the written approval and the identity of the carved-out facilities, and DoD SAPCO must confirm to DCSA which facilities are carved out, so a list exists as an agency record.

Congress has used the money to close the gap for this subject: sections 1687 and 7343 of the FY2024 laws condition defense and intelligence funding for UAP activity on disclosure to the committees and leadership, and since December 2024 an intelligence element may not move a capability from a controlled access programme into a special access programme until notice is given.

Representative Grothman said, a year after Grusch testified, that none of the agencies had been able to substantiate his claims despite members endlessly questioning them inside and outside the SCIF. The board notes this is hard to square with the read-in gate Luna later described.

AARO states that its investigators were granted full access to all pertinent sensitive government programmes, working with the SAP control offices of DoD, the intelligence community and DHS, and the named companies' executives denied the custody allegations on the record. The board's answer, that the SAPCO enterprise itself set what counted as pertinent, is its own inference.

The Department gave stated reasons for keeping inspectors out: the 1965 exclusion rested on the programmes' especially sensitive nature and small number, and DoD refused GAO's 1983 recommendations in part because access by service inspectors would proliferate access. The Lockheed losses are also often overstated: on GAO's figures the unaccounted-for total was 11 documents, Lockheed's own unverified result.

open: Has any Secretary of Defense used the section 119(e) waiver since the annual reports ended in 2021, and for what kind of report?
Has any of the seat holders ever been told of a programme connected with UAP, and would they be free to say so?
Is any UAP-related information protected by Alternative Compensatory Control Measures rather than special access controls, and so outside every reporting statute?
How many carve-outs have been approved, for which contractors, and does the SAPCO-held list of carved-out facilities match DCSA's facility clearance records?
Has any disclosure been made to the committees under sections 1687 or 7343, and what did it cover?

threads.text: The money thread shows the reporting channel narrowing step by step. DoD policy limits a waived programme's budget justification to committee staff directors and its access to the chair, ranking member, staff directors and one security manager of each committee, under the group section 119 created in 1987; section 1687 is Congress overriding that waiver for UAP alone by conditioning the money on wider disclosure. The step joining the classified annex to the accounting rules that let amounts move between lines is the board's inference, and no document links them.
